newsitem.title: UK: European Crude Outlook - Buyers still in control.
newsitem.headline: European Crude Outlook - Buyers still in control.

text.p: A turnaround in the fortunes of North Sea crude sellers hoping to draw a line under a disappointing June looks unlikely as July sales get underway this week, traders said.
Despite a slight upturn in profit margins, refiners' appetite for crude remains poor with last week's buying spree on non-Brent grades triggered mainly by bargain hunting.
"The barrels went to refiners because they were cheap and the contango made storage worthwhile...it wasn't because there was any real demand," said one.
Although expected, an increase in July loadings on Brent and Oseberg as fields come out of maintenance, coupled with plentiful unsold June Brent cargoes, should keep buyers relaxed.
"I think we can expect demand to be slow...there is no real bullish strength behind the market," said one dealer.
The July Brent programme scheduled the equivalent of 40.5 cargoes, two up from June. The Oseberg system is due to load 10 more cargoes in July.
However, traders were still awaiting the July Forties programme which some believed could be curtailed by production problems at the Nelson field.
A trader for a European major was told his cross-month loader would be delayed by seven days due to field maintenance.
"We've seen a few worries about Forties...we might see some end-June buying to cover that," said one North Sea player.
With a differential of just $1.10 a barrel between West Texas Intermediate and Brent for July delivery, the trans-Atlantic arbitrage remains unviable as an outlet for North Sea grades, traders said.
"It's not profitable," said one trader. "There is a VLCC fixed with (a U.S. refiner) but it had some commitments it couldn't unwind."
After a three week slide, international benchmark Dated Brent settled at July Brent -70 cents last week.
Given the contango and the incentive to put barrels in storage, most traders agreed the market had bottomed out, but few were expecting strong gains.

The recent fall in Brent values has halved the August differential between Brent and Dubai to around 60 cents a barrel, clearing the way for a resumption of heavy buying of West African barrels by Asian refiners.
The open arbitrage, which mopped up 200,000 barrels of July-loading barrels last week, should drag West African differentials out of recent doldrums.
A sloppy June market saw Qua Iboe offered down to Dated Brent +20 cents and Bonny light at +30 cents.
The Mediterranean sour market boasted the world's best cracking margins of over $3.00 a barrel last week with benchmark Urals climbing to Dated Brent -$1.00/$1.10.
With rival Iraqi Kirkuk not expected until early July at the earliest, differentials were seen at least holding steady.
"Maybe we won't see it going higher than a dollar, but it is a strong market at the moment," said one trader.
-- Rosalind Russell, London Newsroom +44 171 542 5387
